title: The Approval Gate

protagonist: Priya Nandakumar, AI Operations Lead at Foothill Outfitters

deliverables.text: A complete truth table for Option A's escalation rule and a complete truth table for Option B's escalation rule, each showing all eight true/false combinations of the three conditions defined in Appendix A -- p (amount under threshold), q (tenure over threshold), and r (repeat request) -- with a final column giving each rule's Approve/Escalate output for every row.

A formal conditional ("if...then") statement of Compliance's shared approval rule ("if a request is auto-approved, then..."), plus its converse, inverse, and contrapositive, each written out in full and each given a one-sentence plain-English interpretation of what it would mean operationally for Foothill Outfitters.

A symbolic De Morgan's-Laws derivation of the true logical negation of the shared approval condition (p ∧ q ∧ ¬r), shown step by step, with a written verdict -- citing the specific mismatched row or rows from Challenge 3 (D1)'s truth tables -- on whether Option B's escalation rule is or is not logically equivalent to Option A's.

A monthly-volume table applying Appendix C's request-category counts to each design's truth table (D1) to compute how many requests each design auto-approves versus escalates, followed by a total-expected-monthly-cost calculation for each design -- escalation cost plus expected false-approval loss cost, using Appendix D's figures -- shown step by step for both options.

A one-paragraph written recommendation, using correct logical notation (∧, ∨, ¬, →) throughout, that names which gate design has the lower total expected monthly cost and explicitly addresses why assuming Option B was "the same rule written differently," without building the truth table to check, would have been misleading.

appendices.title: The Approval Gate: Conditions and Thresholds
Monthly Refund Request Volume by Category

balance.argument_a: Option A (The Compound Gate) is the mathematically correct De Morgan's-Laws negation of Compliance's approve rule -- nobody can dispute its logic, since it is derived rather than authored. It escalates 1,600 of the 3,600 monthly requests [MA1] -- every category that fails at least one of the three safety conditions -- at a total cost of 1,600 x $9.00 [MA3] = $14,400.00. A's case is that this is the only design with zero systematic false approvals of unsafe requests: the only category it ever auto-approves (p=T,q=T,r=F, 2,000 requests) is the one category everyone agrees is genuinely safe. Under this case's current numbers A is also the cheaper design overall, despite escalating 106x more requests than B -- its real strength is that avoiding the expected fraud/error loss from under-escalation outweighs its much larger escalation-labor bill.
balance.argument_b: Option B (The Streamlined Gate) escalates only 15 of the 3,600 monthly requests [MA1] -- the single rarest category, where every condition is unfavorable at once -- at a direct escalation cost of just 15 x $9.00 = $135.00. B's real, honest case (not the VP's false 'same policy' claim, which Challenge 3 D3 disproves) is a workload argument: it auto-approves 3,585 requests a month versus A's 2,000, dramatically cutting the escalation-review labor the VP is trying to solve for. Its weakness is that 1,585 of those auto-approvals are requests that fail at least one of Compliance's own safety conditions -- at a 15.14% real fraud rate [S2] and an average $66.00 value at risk [MA4], this produces $15,972.95 in expected total cost, higher than A's, despite B's dramatically lower escalation count.
balance.margin_basis: margin = |cost(loser) - cost(winner)| / cost(loser) x 100 (the corpus's standard margin formula, dividing by the LOSING option's value -- per skills/case-readiness/scripts/tier2_probes.py's probe_sensitivity, which this case's sensitivity_model.py matches exactly once its higher-wins sign convention is unwound), where cost(option) = escalate_count(option) x cost_per_escalation + incorrectly_approved_count(option) x (fraud_rate x avg_value_at_risk). escalate_count(A) = 3,600 - 2,000 = 1,600 (every category except the genuinely-safe p=T,q=T,r=F, per Option A's truth table ¬p ∨ ¬q ∨ r). escalate_count(B) = 15 (only p=F,q=F,r=T, per Option B's truth table ¬p ∧ ¬q ∧ r). incorrectly_approved_count(B) = (3,600 - 15) - 2,000 = 1,585. cost(A) = 1,600 x $9.00 = $14,400.00 (winner, lower cost). cost(B) = 15 x $9.00 + 1,585 x (0.1514 x $66.00) = $135.00 + 1,585 x $9.9924 = $135.00 + $15,837.95 = $15,972.95 (loser, higher cost). margin = |$15,972.95 - $14,400.00| / $15,972.95 x 100 = $1,572.95 / $15,972.95 x 100 = 9.8%. This is within the approved concept's 8-15% margin target. NOTE: the 8 category counts [MA1], the two gate thresholds and repeat-request definition [MA2], the cost per escalation [MA3], and the average value at risk [MA4] are all stated Modeling Assumptions, not sourced figures (only the 15.14% fraud rate [S2] is a real, sourced value used directly) -- this margin is a designed property of the assumptions' chosen values, not an empirical finding.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Monthly refund request volume, by all eight p/q/r categories
modeling_assumptions.basis: No source publishes any specific company's internal AI-agent request logs broken down by condition -- this is proprietary, day-to-day operational data, not a publishable dataset at any confidence grade. Chosen to reflect a realistic pattern for a mid-size retailer: the large majority of requests are fully safe (p=T,q=T,r=F), with smaller counts spread across the seven riskier categories and the rarest category (p=F,q=F,r=F, then p=F,q=F,r=T) being requests that fail multiple or all conditions at once.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: sensitivity_model.py's ±50% flex sweep found every one of the 8 category counts leaves the margin essentially unchanged (~9.8-9.9%) and never flips the winner or breaches the 20% cap -- the total-cost comparison is structurally robust to any single category count moving on its own, because both options' costs scale together with total volume. See sensitivity_disclosure[] -- these 8 params are NOT flagged as unstable.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Dollar amount threshold, tenure threshold, and repeat-request definition
modeling_assumptions.value_used: Amount under $60; tenure over 1 year; repeat = 2nd or more request within a trailing 90-day window
modeling_assumptions.basis: These are Foothill Outfitters' own internal policy thresholds -- no public source publishes the exact dollar figure, tenure length, or lookback window any specific company sets for its own auto-approval gate. Microsoft's own Copilot Studio documentation [S1] confirms real platforms structure approval logic around exactly this kind of explicit numeric threshold and condition set, though its own worked example (a $5,000 expense-approval threshold) is a different domain and scale, not a source for this case's specific dollar figure.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Held fixed in this case's sensitivity testing -- changing a threshold would reshuffle which requests land in which of Appendix C's eight categories, a structural redesign rather than a dial to flex. Not swept by sensitivity_model.py's FLEX[].

modeling_assumptions.basis: No single published source states the exact dollar cost of one manually reviewed refund request. Informed by real, cited ecommerce/retail customer-service cost-per-contact research [S4] spanning roughly $2.70-$15.56 per contact depending on channel and company size, including a Gartner-cited $13.50 average for human-handled ('assisted') contacts generally and Ringly.io's own $6-$12 benchmark assessment (informed by Gorgias ticket-volume data) for smaller ecommerce/retail stores specifically. $9.00 sits within the smaller-retailer range, toward its middle-upper part, since a refund review requires pulling order and customer history rather than answering a simple question.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: This is one of the case's two most sensitive dials. See sensitivity_disclosure[] for the confirmed +/-50% flip/cap-breach finding.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Average dollar value at risk per incorrectly auto-approved, risky refund request
modeling_assumptions.basis: No source publishes Foothill Outfitters' own average refund amount or its own average loss per mishandled request. Set as a company-specific figure near Appendix A's own $60 dollar threshold, since risky requests cluster close to (and sometimes just past) the auto-approval line. Multiplied directly by the sourced 15.14% return-fraud rate [S2] to produce the expected loss per incorrectly approved request used in Challenge 3 (D4).
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: This is the case's single most sensitive dial. See sensitivity_disclosure[] for the confirmed +/-50% flip/cap-breach finding -- a Hero who successfully argues this figure should be materially lower can flip the recommendation to B.

derived.notes: Figures computed from sensitivity_model.py, not restated in case.md (facilitator-only), kept here so FACILITATOR.md's Guide Notes stay checkable against a value of record instead of drifting silently.

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: No public source publishes the exact dollar cost of a manually reviewed refund request at Foothill Outfitters or any comparable real company -- the true figure exists in principle (actual staffing/labor cost records) but is not publicly accessible, and this case's $9.00 value is a documented estimate bounded by real, cited ecommerce/retail cost-per-contact ranges (see modeling_assumptions[MA3]). Tier 2 P5 found this dial genuinely unstable: -50% breaks the 20% cap (54.7% margin, still winner A) and +50% both breaks the cap and FLIPS the winner to B (25.7% margin).

No public source publishes Foothill Outfitters' own average refund amount or its own average loss per mishandled request -- the true figure would exist for a real company's real claims history but is not publicly accessible for this fictional company, and this case's $66.00 value is a documented estimate set near Appendix A's own $60 threshold (see modeling_assumptions[MA4]). Tier 2 P5 found this is the single most flip-sensitive dial in the case: -50% FLIPS the winner to B (44.1% margin, breaks the 20% cap) and +50% breaks the cap in the other direction (39.7% margin, A still wins) -- consistent with modeling_assumptions[MA4].sensitivity.
